meta.description: All cultures for TDE4/DSA4.1 Basic Rules. Talent modifiers are cumulative with race modifiers. Language modifier 'CL-2' means the talent starts at (CL - 2). Automatic SAs are included in the GP cost. Discounted SAs cost half AP/GP (round up). Southern Aventuria data is partially from BRW — marked TBD fields need manual verification from BRW p. 68–70. Enriched with English plain-text cultural descriptions from Wege der Helden (2011), culture chapter pp. 40-84, preserving existing JSON fields and tags. Expanded to include missing cultures from Wege der Helden; existing ids/values preserved where present.

cultures.name: Middenrealm Cities
cultures.description:
Overview:
Middenrealm city culture covers the towns and cities of the central Aventurian heartlands, plus several closely related settlements such as Festum, Vallusa, Lowangen, Riva, Uhdenberg, Kannemünde, and Mhanerhaven. Even a settlement of only a few thousand souls can feel like a metropolis in much of Aventuria, while Gareth is a true urban monster by Aventurian standards.

Life and society:
City life is built around crafts, trade, guild obligations, day labor, service, temples, and the constant pressure of money. Some citizens live comfortably from a trade or profession; others survive as beggars, thieves, informants, debtors, or hired blades. The larger the city, the more opportunities it offers, but also the more dangerous its alleys become.

Worldview and religion:
Most citizens follow the Twelvegods, but urban people are usually more tolerant of foreign customs and religions than villagers. Ingerimm, Travia, Phex, Praios, Boron, and the local patron deity all matter depending on city type. Urban citizens often look down on rural folk, especially in large commercial or scholarly centers.

Customs and appearance:
Clothing is usually practical: trousers, dresses, tunics, shirts, vests, cloaks, hoods, and work clothes for artisans. Wealthier citizens follow local fashions. Many townsfolk carry a dagger; guild militias and civic duties may teach crossbow, halberd, or similar practical weapons.

Roleplaying notes:
A city-born hero should know a district, a guild, a temple, a market, or a circle of useful contacts. They are adaptable, socially alert, and more likely to understand written law, trade, bribes, rumors, and the unwritten rules of urban survival.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 40-41; BRW p. 60-61

cultures.name: Middenrealm Rural Population
cultures.description:
Overview:

Characters from this culture should be grounded in the everyday pressures of their homeland: livelihood, status, family or clan ties, expected duties, local law, and the practical skills needed to survive there. Use the culture's region and social order to decide whether the hero thinks first as a citizen, villager, nomad, sailor, clansperson, slave, noble, craftsperson, warrior, or outsider.

Belief and custom are part of the culture rather than decoration. Twelvegods piety, Rastullah faith, spirit beliefs, elven harmony, dwarven Angrosh devotion, ork strength codes, goblin tribal customs, or Achaz ancestral memory should shape what the hero considers normal, shameful, sacred, or dangerous.

cultures.name: Andergast / Nostria
cultures.description:
Overview:
Andergast and Nostria are two small, backward-looking forest kingdoms along the Ingval and Tommel. Outsiders mock them as rustic, poor, and hopelessly old-fashioned, but their people have survived generations of war, scarcity, wild country, and northern threats.

Life and society:
Most people live from farming, forest work, hunting, small crafts, and improvised repairs. The local nobility is famously tangled in family connections, and important positions often fall to some cousin, in-law, or distant relative. Although the old war has formally cooled into a shaky truce, distrust and border grudges remain part of everyday life.

Worldview and religion:
The Twelvegods are known and honored, but older nature beliefs remain strong, especially in Andergast. Peraine is important among the rural population, Efferd on the coast, and druidic Sumucults still survive in the depths of the forests. Andergast is notably patriarchal compared with many Middenrealm lands.

Customs and appearance:
The forest has high cultural value, and many festivals, sayings, and taboos center on woods, spirits, animals, and old local customs. Practical clothing, reused equipment, and improvised tools are common. Veterans and peasant levies often fight with adapted tools such as war scythes, flails, axes, and spears.

Roleplaying notes:
Play Andergasters and Nostrians as stubborn, suspicious of novelty, frugal, and astonishingly resourceful. They collect anything that might one day be useful and can often solve a crisis with rope, resin, nails, and a deeply held conviction that new ideas are probably dangerous.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 42-44; BRW p. 61-62

cultures.name: Bornland
cultures.description:
Overview:
The Bornland is a northern noble republic of deep forests, long winters, hard travel, and sharp social divisions. Festum is its great city, but much of the countryside, especially Seweria, is ruled by Bronnjars whose authority over peasants can be harsh and absolute.

Life and society:
Most commoners live by agriculture, animal husbandry, fishing, woodcraft, and endurance. Serfdom is stronger here than almost anywhere else in Aventuria. The nobility gathers periodically in Festum to choose an Adelsmarschall, but even a penniless noble retains political dignity that no commoner can easily reach.

Worldview and religion:
Bornlanders follow the Twelvegods. Peraine and Travia are loved by the rural population; in winter, Firun is approached through Ifirn for mercy. Among nobles, Rondra often overshadows Praios. Protective images, amulets, saints' tablets, and household piety are common.

Customs and appearance:
Winter shapes everything. Warm clothing, fur, heavy food, and strong drink are part of the culture; only Thorwal rivals the Bornland for drinking customs. Hunting is a noble privilege, and commoners who poach or even interfere with noble game risk brutal punishment.

Roleplaying notes:
A Bornlander is often friendly, stubborn, melancholic, old-fashioned, and deeply aware of winter and hierarchy. A commoner may fear the Bronnjar more than bandits; a noble may view softer southern rule as dangerously sentimental.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 44-45; BRW p. 62-64

cultures.name: Horasian Empire
cultures.description:
Overview:
The Horasian Empire, centered on the Liebliches Feld, is the dominant power of Aventuria's western coast and the self-proclaimed heir of old Bosparan. It sees itself as refined, free, learned, fashionable, and far superior to the supposedly barbaric lands around it.

Life and society:
The region is unusually urbanized for Aventuria, rich in towns, ports, manufactories, farms, scholars, merchants, and ambitious citizens. Farmers can prosper from the fertile land, while city dwellers live from craft, trade, service, scholarship, and wage labor. Beggars and the urban poor still exist, but so do powerful merchant princes and patrician families.

Worldview and religion:
Horasian culture prizes intellectual freedom, elegance, pleasure, commerce, and public reputation. Hesinde's wisdom, Rahja's joy, Phexian trade, and civic pride all shape public life. Slavery is strongly rejected in the core Horasian lands. Horasians are often tolerant of foreign ideas, but also famously arrogant.

Customs and appearance:
Fashion matters. Vinsalt, Kuslik, Grangor, Belhanka, and other cities set tastes in clothing, wine, art, fencing, salons, and manners. Public festivals, theatrical life, scholarly congresses, noble houses, wealthy burghers, and urban politics give the culture a sophisticated tone.

Roleplaying notes:
A Horasian hero is educated, polished, socially ambitious, and used to complex rules of status. They may admire liberty and refinement while casually assuming that other Aventurians are provincial.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 47-49; BRW p. 64-65

cultures.name: Tulamidian City-States
cultures.notes: Full talent table partially derived from spec; verify against BRW p. 65 for complete data. The +1 RM modifier applies specifically to heroes who are casters (Vollzauberer or Viertelzauberer).
cultures.description:
Overview:
The Tulamidian City-States are old, wealthy, hard-edged urban cultures shaped by trade, rivalry, magic, and the pride of ancient civilization. Their citizens often see themselves as sharper, more cultured, and more clever than rural Fellachen.

Life and society:
Status depends less on hereditary nobility and more on wealth, influence, and cultural belonging. A powerful family can rule because it keeps its fortune; a lost caravan may ruin a house. Crafts, trade, gardens, livestock, caravan business, scholarship, begging, theft, and street robbery all exist side by side in crowded, twisting streets.

Worldview and religion:
The cities share many Tulamidian customs with Mhanadistan, but each city also has local cults and sacred traditions. Rashdul honors Boron strongly, Thalusa emphasizes Praios and Efferd, Fasar keeps older city gods, heroes, saints, and half-divine powers alive in public memory.

Customs and appearance:
Urban Tulamides have access to exotic cloth, foreign fashions, jewelry, and many weapons. Practicality often wins over cultural purity. In politics and business, the clever swindler may be admired more than the poor honest man.

Roleplaying notes:
A city-state Tulamide is quick, proud, suspicious, profit-minded, and trained to protect their back. Away from home, they may slowly learn to trust companions, but their first instinct is to ask who benefits and who is trying to cheat whom.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 53-54; BRW p. 65

cultures.name: Novadis (Men / Achmad'sunni)
cultures.description:
Overview:
This entry represents male Novadis of the desert tribes, especially the Beni Novad shaped by the Khôm. For many Novadis, belonging is as much a religious commitment to Rastullah as a matter of ancestry.

Life and society:
Desert Novadis live as herding nomads or oasis dwellers. Horses are prized above camels and are treated as treasures of tribe, wealth, and honor. Urban or settled Rastullah-believers may use Tulamidian City-State values or oasis variants, but the desert tribes are defined by riding, navigation, endurance, and strict custom.

Worldview and religion:
Novadis worship Rastullah alone. They acknowledge the Twelvegods but view them as rebellious servants who rose too high during Rastullah's long sleep. The Ninety-Nine Holy Laws guide faith, society, honor, food, gender roles, and war.

Customs and appearance:
Some tribes greet strangers with a staged mounted charge, testing courage before granting hospitality. The shadow-fight is a secretive, partly religious martial exercise against an imagined foe, often practiced with a Khunchomer blade. Men dominate public society; women have limited rights after marriage, though rare Achmad'sunni avengers exist.

Roleplaying notes:
A male Novadi hero should feel proud, devout, direct, and bound by laws of honor and hospitality. He is a rider, survivor, and believer first, and will often judge foreigners by courage, self-control, and respect for Rastullah's law.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 54-55; BRW p. 66

cultures.name: Novadis (Women)
cultures.description:
Overview:
This entry represents female Novadis from the desert tribes. They share the same Khôm-shaped faith, hardship, hospitality, and tribal identity as the men, but their social position is sharply restricted by patriarchal custom.

Life and society:
Novadi women help sustain clan life through household management, animal care, craft, healing knowledge, oral tradition, and survival skills. An unmarried girl may enjoy some freedom; after marriage she is usually placed under her husband's authority along with much of the household property.

Worldview and religion:
Rastullah's faith and the Ninety-Nine Holy Laws frame daily life. A Novadi woman is expected to know law, custom, family duty, and reputation. In rare cases, an unmarried woman may become an Achmad'sunni, a daughter of vengeance, taking up a role normally closed to her.

Customs and appearance:
Modesty, head coverings, clan identity, hospitality, and strict gender expectations shape presentation. Women may not always stand in public as warriors, but within the tribe they can be keepers of memory, practical authority, healing, negotiation, and endurance.

Roleplaying notes:
A female Novadi hero can be devout, proud, resilient, sharp-tongued, and very aware of the limits placed on her. Adventuring may represent exile, vengeance, rare permission, rebellion, or a sacred duty that overrides ordinary expectations.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 54-55; BRW p. 66

cultures.name: Thorwal
cultures.description:
Overview:
Thorwal is a free, seafaring northern culture famous for fearless sailors, raiders, traders, brawlers, storytellers, and loud hospitality. Thorwalers live along the Sea of Seven Winds but are found in harbors throughout Aventuria.

Life and society:
The heart of Thorwalian life is the Ottajasko, a ship-community of roughly forty men and women who sail together in summer and share longhouses in winter. Hetmen and Hetwomen are chosen leaders, not distant monarchs. Farming and herding exist, but the culture's reputation rests on ships, raids, trade, courage, and independence.

Worldview and religion:
Swafnir, the divine whale, stands at the center of Thorwalian faith, locked in mythic struggle against the sea-serpent Hranngar. Many Thorwalers still recognize parts of the Twelvegods tradition, especially Efferd, Rondra, Firun/Ifirn, and Travia, but Swafnir's cult is dominant. Slavery is hated, as are slavers and whalers.

Customs and appearance:
Drinking, bathing houses, boasts, feasts, ship songs, feuds, and public courage all matter. Gender equality is normal: a woman may sail while a man keeps the household. Thorwalers are often open toward other peoples, though quick to anger when freedom or honor is challenged.

Roleplaying notes:
A Thorwaler should feel physically bold, emotionally direct, freedom-loving, and suspicious of excessive hierarchy. They make excellent sailors, fighters, mercenaries, pirates, explorers, and loud troublemakers with strong loyalty to their crew.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 58-59; BRW p. 67-68

cultures.name: Southern Aventuria
cultures.notes: Data partially estimated from spec doc and BRW context. Verify full talent table from BRW p. 68–70 before use in production. Some talent modifiers may differ.
cultures.description:
Overview:
Southern Aventuria is a mixed coastal culture formed from old Tulamidian settlements, later Middenrealm colonists, local Waldmenschen influence, and the politics of independent city-states, Al'Anfa, and distant colonial powers.

Life and society:
Most people live in harbor cities, old colonies, plantations, or coastal settlements; the deep interior has few large human settlements apart from places such as Mirham. In practice, the powerful are wealthy trade lords, officers, scholars, and Granden, while the free middle strata, the Fanas, stand above the poor and enslaved.

Worldview and religion:
The Twelvegods are widespread, but interpretations vary sharply. The Al'Anfan Boron rite is especially famous, while some cities restrict Praios or Phex worship. Nature cults, demon-influenced practices, Rastullah, Rur and Gror, and many local beliefs may overlap. Firun is almost unknown in everyday southern religion.

Customs and appearance:
Slavery and human trafficking are common in many southern states, though Brabak, Hôt-Alem, and some Bornland or Horasian colonies reject them. Corruption, decadence, political plots, gladiatorial games, drugs, poisonings, and gambling are part of the cultural reputation, especially around Al'Anfa and Chorhop.

Roleplaying notes:
A southern Aventurian hero is adapted to heat, ports, money, danger, and complicated loyalties. They may be charming, pragmatic, cynical, proud of their city, and used to seeing law, faith, and morality bend under wealth and power.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 68-69; BRW p. 68-70

cultures.name: Lea Elves

automatic_disadvantages.note: Two areas per BRW: possessions (ownership); religious devotion (blindly follows teachings)

cultures.leittalente_note: Talents marked is_leittalent are Lead Talents (Leittalente) under the Elvish World View disadvantage. They advance more cheaply and have additional narrative obligations.
cultures.description:
Overview:
Lea Elves, or Auelfen, are the elves whose lands lie closest to human settlement. Most still live in clans away from larger towns, especially along rivers north of the Salamander Stones, though Gerasim and Kvirasim are rare examples of larger elven settlements.

Life and society:
Lea Elves commonly live in hidden tree or stilt-like settlements in river meadows. Hunting and fishing provide their foundation, supplemented by fruit, herbs, limited trade, and highly refined crafts such as bowmaking, fur work, carving, music, and decorative art. Strict human-style professions and hierarchies are alien to them; each member is expected to serve the community in many ways.

Worldview and religion:
Like other elves, they know of human gods but do not worship them. They honor the balance of Nurti and Zerzal, becoming and passing, life and death. Wealth in coins or metal is strange to them; beauty, song, a well-made bow, a carved flute, and harmony with life are far more meaningful.

Customs and appearance:
Elven love, celebration, music, dance, and judgment differ deeply from human law. They have no courts in the human sense; social harmony and the opinion of the clan are stronger than written statutes. The harshest punishment is exclusion from communal perception. Clothing is self-made from leather or Bausch cloth, often dyed or decorated with feathers, fur, embroidery, teeth, and natural colors.

Roleplaying notes:
A Lea Elf should feel graceful, curious, musical, communal, and quietly alien. They may deal with humans more often than other elves, but still struggle with greed, ownership, hierarchy, rigid law, and the idea that metal wealth matters.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 74-76; BRW p. 71-72

cultures.name: Anvil Dwarves
cultures.description:
Overview:
Anvil Dwarves are the archetypal Angroshim of human imagination: soot-darkened skin, chainmail, heavy axes, loud drinking, stubborn pride, and a readiness to leave the mountain for a good fight. They go adventuring more often than many other dwarven peoples.

Life and society:
Their main homeland is the mountain kingdom of Waldwacht in the Anvil Mountains, with related clans in other ranges. Their underground halls resemble furnished mines lit by forgefire. Work, drinking, tales of ancestors, clan loyalty, and craft define daily life.

Worldview and religion:
Anvil Dwarves worship Angrosch as creator and divine master of the forge; some clans also place Rondra beside him as a warlike consort. The enemy image of the Dragon includes actual dragons, destructive sorcery, and the works of the Nameless One. Smithing is not merely a trade, but worship.

Customs and appearance:
They value independence, clan self-reliance, weaponsmithing, battle courage, endurance, feasting, and ritualized excess. Chainmail is both clothing and heirloom. Typical weapons include heavy warhammers, double-bladed axes, short swords, heavy daggers, and excellent crossbows.

Roleplaying notes:
An Anvil Dwarf is not just a short warrior. Emphasize alien patience, clan memory, love of stone and forge, distrust of dragons and dark magic, blunt honesty, stubbornness, and the melancholy fact that human friends die almost as soon as one grows used to them.
cultures.source: Wege der Helden (2011) p. 81-82; BRW p. 71
